summary: This Informational document defines an operational convention using the underscored DNS node name "_for-sale" to show a domain name is available for purchase. It can be deployed without disrupting existing operations, even if the domain is in use.

eli5.summary: A "for sale" sign for a web address, placed in the internet phone book.

questions: how to mark a domain for sale in dns
how to sell a domain name with dns
subtitle: A simple DNS record to advertise that a domain name is for sale.

tldr.problem: When a registered domain name becomes available for purchase, interested buyers have no standard way to find out. Existing domain-lookup tools like WHOIS show that a name is registered but not whether the owner is willing to sell.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 10023 defines a simple operational convention using an underscored DNS leaf node named "_for-sale" with TXT records following a standardized format. The records contain a version tag and optional content tags describing the sale (contact URI, free-text information, asking price, or opaque codes).
tldr.outcome: Domain holders can now signal availability for sale directly in the DNS without disrupting existing operations, enabling brokers and interested parties to discover and potentially automate engagement with sellers.

today: RFC 10023, published in July 2026, is an Informational RFC representing IETF consensus. The _for-sale underscored node name has been registered with IANA in the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry, making it an established operational convention for the Internet community.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
Well-established services like WHOIS and RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) let you check whether a domain name is registered, but they do not tell you whether it is actually for sale. A domain might be registered but its owner may never want to sell it. Some brokers offer services connecting buyers and sellers, but these services are limited when the domain owner has not explicitly marked the name as for sale.

RFC 10023 introduces a simple, immediately deployable solution: a reserved underscored leaf node name called _for-sale placed in a domain's DNS zone. This convention allows a domain holder to add a TXT record under _for-sale.example.com to signal that example.com is available for purchase. The signal can be turned on and off at will, and it requires no protocol changes or modifications to existing infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Instead of hunting through different websites to find if someone wants to sell their domain name, you can just look for a special "_for-sale" marker in the DNS. If it's there, the domain is for sale.

sections.title: The TXT Record Format
sections.content:
Each _for-sale TXT record must begin with a version tag, currently v=FORSALE1;. This mandatory version tag allows processors to distinguish valid _for-sale records from unrelated TXT records, and it paves the way for future versions if the format evolves.

After the version tag comes optional content in tag=value format. The RFC defines four standardized content tags. A single TXT record MUST contain at most one content tag-value pair, though an RRset (the complete set of TXT records for _for-sale) may contain multiple records with different content tags. Each tag-value pair in the RRset MUST be unique.
sections.eli5: The record starts with "v=FORSALE1;" to show it's a for-sale marker. Then you can add information like a web link, a phone number, a price, or a code that you and the buyer understand.

sections.title: Four Content Tag Types
sections.content:
fcod (code) contains an opaque value meaningful only to systems that understand its semantics, such as a registry-generated code that redirects to a for-sale URL. A registry might generate a unique code that lets it redirect visitors to the correct sales page without exposing the URI directly in DNS. ftxt (text) holds concise human-readable information, such as "Call for info" or eligibility criteria. This is intended for display to humans rather than automated processing.

furi (URI) contains a single human-readable and machine-parsable URI that interested parties can visit for more information. Recommended schemes are https, http, mailto, and tel. fval (value) specifies an asking price using an uppercase currency code (like USD, EUR, or even cryptocurrency codes like BTC) followed by a numeric amount (e.g., fval=EUR500). This provides structured, machine-parsable pricing information without modifying existing WHOIS systems.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of information you can include: a secret code for your broker, plain text for humans, a web link, or a price with currency. You can pick what makes sense for your situation.

sections.title: Practical Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC recommends short TTLs (time-to-live values of 3600 seconds or less) for _for-sale records to reduce the risk of outdated information misleading potential buyers into thinking a domain is still available when it has already sold. The operational convention works with the global DNS and does not apply to special-use domain names like .onion or infrastructure TLDs like .arpa.

A _for-sale record requires the domain name to be resolvable in the DNS. It may not be available during registration redemption periods or when DNSSEC validation fails. Processors interpreting these records must be liberal in what they accept but should sanitize dangerous content. For example, if publishing URI values on a website, processors must validate and sanitize them to prevent cross-site scripting or SQL injection attacks. Automatically following URIs without user confirmation creates security risks and is forbidden.
sections.eli5: Update the record quickly when the domain sells so people don't waste time contacting you. Be careful about what links you include so they don't trick anyone. Don't automatically click links for users.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
Publishing contact information in the DNS creates security and privacy trade-offs. The _for-sale signal is publicly visible to anyone querying the DNS, potentially exposing the intent to sell a domain name. This information is at risk of being scraped for email addresses and phone numbers, leading to spam and unwanted contact.

Domain holders may list artificially low prices, so processors displaying asking prices should show disclaimers like "Price indicative only—verify with seller." Malicious domain holders could publish URIs pointing to phishing pages, malware, or misleading content, causing reputational damage to parties that display the information without proper validation. The RFC emphasizes that parsing and publishing information from _for-sale records requires careful validation of characters and formats, with possible mitigations including output sanitisation, maintaining curated lists of URIs, or applying URI reputation checks before display.
sections.eli5: Once you post that your domain is for sale, spammers might contact you. Be honest about the price. And if you include a link, make sure it's a real, safe link so people trust whoever displays it.

data.title: Sample DNS records
data.code:
_for-sale IN TXT "v=FORSALE1;furi=https://example.com/forsale"
_for-sale IN TXT "v=FORSALE1;ftxt=Contact: +1-201-555-0123"
_for-sale IN TXT "v=FORSALE1;fval=USD750"
_for-sale IN TXT "v=FORSALE1;fcod=EXCO-aHR0cHM..."
